title: Redwood technical deep dive - OOMs, timeouts, CUDA, retry semantics
summary: Deep dive into a series of OOMs and CUDA-related timeouts observed during internal benchmarks. Discussed root causes (batching spikes, KV cache eviction, quantization edge-cases), retry semantics and backoff strategies, and safe defaults for private/VPC deployments. Agreed next steps: send detailed logs, share patch that changes batching heuristic, run targeted repros on customer's on-prem nodes.
action_items: Sofia Patel: Share benchmark spreadsheet and logs (due: 2026-04-13)
Miguel Alvarez: Prepare a patch with conservative batching heuristic + documentation (due: 2026-04-17)
Tom Reynolds (customer): Run repro on 3-node on-prem cluster and send results (due: 2026-04-20)
Li Wei (customer): Provide VM/GPU details + KMS/network config (due: 2026-04-14)
next_steps: Redwood -> send security notes and per-model quantization caveats
Customer -> schedule follow-up run (30-45 min) the week of 4/20
SE -> open internal RFC for retry/backoff defaults and KV cache tuning
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-04-10
Start: 14:00 PDT
Duration: 55m
Attendees: Sofia Patel (Redwood AE), Miguel Alvarez (Redwood SE), Asha Menon (CTO, DataBridge Health), Tom Reynolds (ML Eng), Li Wei (Infra)

Summary (auto): deep technical triage on intermittent OOMs and CUDA timeouts during batch workload runs.

[00:00] Sofia: hey everyone thanks for joining, we'll kick off, miguel and i will run through what we saw in the logs and then triage with you on the on-prem repros
[00:12] Asha: yeah thanks, trying to keep this focused, last week we had two production incidents after the nightly batch where some tasks hit OOMs and others timed out, impact was small but we want root cause
[00:25] Miguel: ok quick note - we've got the logs you shared, and there are really two failure modes: one is CUDA OOMs during high-concurrency batches, second is long tail timeouts where the kernel seems to hang and the request hits the client-side deadline
[00:38] Tom: i can confirm, on the 3-node on-prem cluster we saw memory creep across iterations, and occasionally the KV cache eviction spikes right before the OOM
[00:51] Li: our infra notes - gpus are A100 40GB, cuda 12.1 drivers, host memory is 512GB, docker runtime is runc, network is an internal VPC with strict egress rules
[01:05] Miguel: okay that helps - two quick suspects: batching heuristic that allows a burst to increase effective batch size, and quantized kernels that hit alignment edge cases for certain layer dims causing extra scratch memory or fallback paths
[01:18] Asha: can you explain the fallback path bit? we saw "cooda error" in the transcript, is that the CUDA fallback?
[01:25] Miguel: yeah sorry i said "cooda" - bad transcribe - what happens is when a quantized kernel isn't supported on a particular compute path the runtime falls back to a slower, memory-heavy path which increases memory pressure. sometimes that fallback path isn't accounted for in our batch sizing math
[01:40] Sofia: quick Q: are these spikes correlated with particular models or sequence lengths?
[01:45] Tom: mostly the longer sequences, 1k+ tokens, and when we had concurrent requests from internal scoring jobs + user traffic - spikes matched the peak concurrency windows
[01:58] Miguel: that aligns. the KV cache behavior also matters: if prefix caching is warmed then repeated requests have lower cost, but if there's cache thrashing (evictions + reloads) the effective memory per request jumps
[02:12] Li: we saw a bunch of eviction logs right before the OOMs. i think the cache size was tuned to default and might be too small for our workload
[02:25] Asha: is there a way to force more conservative batching? we prefer predictable latency over micro-perf gains
[02:30] Miguel: absolutely - we can flip the batching heuristic to cap effective batch byte-size and to keep more aggressive per-request timeouts. i can prepare a patch that reduces max batch size from the default of 4k tokens to 2k tokens for your heavy models
[02:45] Tom: that would be great. also about timeouts - some of our clients use client-side deadlines of 10s, and then the SDK retries briefly which causes queuing, and then we see cascades
[02:58] Sofia: this is where retry semantics matter. our current default is an exponential backoff with jitter but the initial retry window is 200ms which can add up under contention
[03:12] Miguel: suggestion: for heavy/tail-prone routes use no immediate retry on 500-like internal errors, instead mark the request for slow-retry with 1s base backoff and a cap. also consider circuit-breaker so we fail fast rather than queue long
[03:30] Asha: can the platform expose circuit-breaker controls per-route in the private deployment? in our security model operations want to set per-route SLOs
[03:38] Sofia: yes, in our Dedicated/Private config you can provide per-route policies - the UI and config are slightly different for on-prem but we do support per-route backoff and circuit settings
[03:50] Li: are there any GPU driver versions that are known-bad? we are trying to reconcile driver 12.1 vs 11.x differences
[03:58] Miguel: good Q - we have seen subtle kernel regressions across driver versions. A100 on 12.1 is usually fine but certain fused kernels behave differently. we recommend a compatibility matrix; i'll include the exact driver/gcc/cuDNN combos we validated
[04:15] Tom: another weird thing - sometimes we saw "timeout waiting for cuContext" and logs said kernel launch stalled, then the runtime retried and then OOM'd
[04:25] Miguel: "timeout waiting for cuContext" usually means the GPU got saturated with pending kernels; either there's a runaway loop generating kernels, or a long-tail kernel grabbed the device for many ms. packing more small kernels can spike the command queue and starve memory reclamation
[04:40] Sofia: let's talk KV cache specifics: does your workload use long prefix caching across calls or per-request contexts?
[04:48] Tom: we do both - user chat sessions have long-lived cache per session and the scoring pipeline sometimes pulls in many prefixes for rerank jobs
[04:55] Miguel: that pattern explains eviction spikes: if many sessions have large KV footprints and they're all touched during scoring, the runtime's cache LRU gets hammered. we have tunables: cache_max_bytes, per-session cache cap, and an eviction policy. default is LRU with approximate byte accounting - which can be off due to quantization overheads
[05:12] Li: quantization overheads? i thought quantization saved memory
[05:15] Miguel: usually it does, but some quantization paths allocate additional temporary buffers for dequantize/accumulate or for fallback kernels. e.g., 4-bit indices may need extra scratch. if a fallback happens to a float kernel, you get both quantized storage and float scratch temporarily
[05:30] Asha: so the combination of high concurrency, long sequences, and fallback kernels is the perfect storm
[05:36] Miguel: exactly. our early repro shows that when batch size increases beyond the safe threshold and a single layer triggers fallback, the extra scratch pushes the total beyond GPU memory causing OOM
[05:50] Tom: what's the diagnostic approach - how do we prove it's the fallback?
[05:55] Miguel: we add a flag to the runtime to log kernel selection decisions and scratch alloc sizes per request, then run controlled batches varying seq len and quantization flags. we can reproduce locally and on your on-prem if you provide similar load patterns
[06:10] Sofia: quick operational note: we'll need the logs with timestamps, gpu memory snapshots (nvidia-smi dmon / nvidia-smi --query), and coredump / tensor sizes if available. we'll annotate the spreadsheet
[06:25] Tom: i can collect nvidia-smi snapshots, docker stats, and the process-level pmap dumps, we'll share to the sheet you mentioned
[06:32] Miguel: perfect - also include the model config: attention dims, layer sizes, and whether you're running fused attention kernels or not
[06:42] Li: about VPC rules - our egress is restricted, will that affect the private control plane operations or logging?
[06:50] Sofia: for Private/VPC we support a local control plane with optional outbound telemetry; if you have strict egress you can run fully air-gapped and we provide a bundle with logs/metrics authorship. some of our automated telemetry features require egress but those are optional
[07:05] Asha: we prefer minimal egress; can the runtime still collect per-request kernel metrics locally?
[07:10] Miguel: yes metrics are local; we can persist them to a local time series. we just won't send to redwood cloud unless you enable it
[07:18] Tom: back to retries - how does Redwood handle idempotency? our requests sometimes have side-effectful calls downstream
[07:25] Sofia: our SDK supports idempotency keys and the platform has idempotent-route flags; we recommend enabling idempotency for routes where retries could cause duplicates. for non-idempotent ops we suggest conservative retry policy or client-coordinated retries
[07:40] Miguel: also a note on partial responses: for streaming responses we support chunk-level acknowledgments so you can resume from the last ack on reconnection instead of full retry
[07:50] Asha: good to know. can you elaborate on the specific metrics to watch in the console to flag this pattern?
[07:57] Miguel: watch GPU memory used vs reserved, kernel queue depth, time in queue, and per-request scratch allocation. in the console you can set alerts on memory high-water events and kernel stall thresholds
[08:10] Tom: do you have a recommended backoff config? we tried 200/500ms and it still fails under load
[08:16] Miguel: recommended for heavy models: no immediate retry on 5xx internal errors; start with base 800ms, factor 2, jitter 0.25, max 6s, and enable circuit-breaker at 30% error rate over 1m window
[08:32] Li: would that affect user-perceived latency too much?
[08:36] Sofia: it's a tradeoff: you avoid cascading queuing but some individual requests will retry slower. for customer-facing low-latency routes you can keep aggressive retries but cap concurrency and use dedicated capacity
[08:50] Tom: dedicated capacity - could that isolate us? we were considering Redwood Dedicated for some models
[08:55] Sofia: yes Dedicated gives you reserved GPUs and isolation; that reduces noisy neighbor risk and gives predictable throughput. it's more expensive but for SLO-critical routes it pays off
[09:05] Asha: if we go Dedicated, do we still need KV cache tuning?
[09:09] Miguel: yes, cache tuning still matters, but the headroom is higher so the same workload is less likely to OOM. still tune eviction and per-session caps
[09:18] Tom: about quantization - we're using a 4-bit quantization for some models, should we roll back?
[09:24] Miguel: not necessarily. quantization provides big memory wins but you should test fallback frequency. we can run A/B with quant and float, measure fallback rate and scratch allocation. if fallback is > 1% of requests, that's suspicious and we look for kernel bugs or alignment issues
[09:41] Asha: is fallback rate something the runtime can expose in metrics?
[09:44] Miguel: yes we'll add a metric for fallback_count by kernel variant, and expose per-model fallback_rate in the console
[09:52] Li: the logs showed some lines mentioning "kv cache thrash" and "alloc failed: out of memory" with similar timestamps - seems synchronous
[09:59] Miguel: that's consistent with eviction-triggered reloads where multiple threads attempt to repopulate the cache causing temporary spike in live memory usage
[10:12] Tom: could a single request trigger multiple cache reloads?
[10:16] Miguel: yes if it references many sessions/prefixes and cache misses cascade; we have a prefetch/lock strategy to mitigate, but it depends on how your scorer pulls prefixes (it may pull them in serial triggering repeated evictions)
[10:30] Sofia: operational mitigation options recap: reduce max batch size, increase per-session cache cap, set conservative retry/backoff, enable circuit breaker, run repro with kernel logging
[10:40] Asha: are there known fixes on the roadmap? we saw recent releases mentioning kernel memory accounting improvements
[10:46] Miguel: yes, upcoming runtime patch improves scratch accounting and adds a safer fallback path that frees quantized buffers earlier. we'll provide a backport for private deployments if you need it
[10:58] Tom: can we get a patch and test it in parallel? we can schedule a maintenance window
[11:02] Miguel: yes i'll prepare a patch branch and a small docker image with debug flags enabled, plus a script to run the repro harness. we'll include instructions for collecting kernel-selection logs
[11:12] Li: for on-prem, do we need to change driver versions? we prefer not to touch production drivers without justification
[11:18] Miguel: understood - we'll provide a compatibility matrix and recommend trying the patch first; only upgrade drivers if the patch doesn't cover the fallback path
[11:28] Asha: one more question on retries: when the runtime retries internally should it be visible to the client? we're trying to correlate client logs with server retries
[11:36] Sofia: we can emit an event in logs for internal retries and expose it in per-request trace so you can correlate via request_id
[11:44] Tom: excellent. that will help debugging. also, please include guidance for SDK settings for idempotency and deadlines
[11:50] Miguel: will do. we'll add recommended SDK configs per scenario in the doc we send
[11:58] Asha: what does a typical repro plan look like?
[12:02] Miguel: short: 1) enable kernel selection logs, 2) run controlled batches with seq lenses 256/512/1024/1536, 3) toggle quantization on/off, 4) vary concurrency 1-32, 5) collect nvidia-smi snapshots every second and runtime scratch logs
[12:22] Tom: we'll start with seq 1024 at concurrency 8 which matched the issue window
[12:28] Li: and we'll provide host settings and any container limits we set so you can match exactly
[12:34] Sofia: ok let's capture next steps - miguel will prepare patch and logging image, sofia will share spreadsheet with log schema, customer will run repro and share findings, and we'll reconvene after initial run
[12:50] Miguel: quick note - there may be transcription noise in the logs for product names like "Redwood Dedicated" sometimes transcribed as "Redwood dedicate" in your notes, just flag it
[12:58] Asha: ha noted. also we may need SOC2 / compliance notes for running debug images in our environment
[13:04] Sofia: we'll attach the compliance checklist; for Private we have a minimal compliance bundle for debug images and a process for approval
[13:12] Tom: any ETA on the patch?
[13:15] Miguel: i'll target an initial branch by 4/17, docs and image by 4/20
[13:22] Li: great. can you share the patch link in the spreadsheet? that makes tracking easier
[13:27] Sofia: yes we'll add links. quick final Q - are there any safety nets to avoid OOM vs crash? like auto-degrade to smaller model variant when memory high-water?
[13:36] Miguel: we have a fallback routing policy - if memory pressure crosses a threshold we can route to a lighter model or quantized variant, or shed non-critical requests. for Private you can configure those thresholds
[13:52] Asha: that sounds useful. we'll discuss which routes are critical vs best-effort
[13:57] Sofia: ok wrapping up - recap in notes and action items in the sheet. thanks everyone
[14:02] Tom: thanks, appreciate the help
[14:05] Miguel: thanks all, we'll follow up with the branch and logs
[14:10] [END TRANSCRIPT]
